summary: Benin is visa-free for citizens of every African country and free to enter for ECOWAS nationals, while all other visitors apply online for the official e-Visa (evisa.bj) before travel. There is no visa on arrival. Yellow fever vaccination is recommended, but vaccination cards are no longer checked at the border.

payments.text: Canada's travel advice describes a cash-based economy: credit cards are generally accepted in major hotels but rarely in restaurants and other shops, and ATMs that take foreign cards are found in banks and some large hotels but are rare outside the major cities.

safety.text: Southern Benin, including Cotonou, is calmer, but street crime, theft and mugging are common in Cotonou and carjacking is a risk on roads outside towns. In the north the FCDO advises against all travel to the W and Pendjari national parks, their hunting zones and the area between Park W and the Niger border, because of terrorist attacks and kidnapping, and against all but essential travel to the rest of the Alibori and Atacora departments and to the area between the RNIE 2 highway (Tchaourou–Malanville) and the Nigerian border.

tips.text: Avoid the areas bordering Burkina Faso and Niger, including Pendjari and W national parks — jihadist groups have attacked and kidnapped in the far north.
Apply for the eVisa only on the official portal (evisa.bj) — third-party sites charge steep mark-ups for the same document.

Vaccination cards, including the yellow fever certificate, have not been checked at Benin's borders since September 2026, but the vaccine is still recommended and checks can return without notice in a health emergency — keep your yellow card with your passport.
Carry CFA franc cash outside Cotonou. Canada's travel advice says credit cards are rarely accepted beyond major hotels, and ATMs that take foreign cards are rare outside the major cities.
Canada's travel advice says most zémidjan motorcycle taxis are unregistered and are sometimes targeted by violent crime, particularly at night, and advises using only official car taxis.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Benin?
faq.answer: Citizens of all African countries enter visa-free for up to 90 days, and ECOWAS nationals enjoy full free movement. Everyone else — including EU, UK and US passport holders — must apply online for the official e-Visa at evisa.bj before travel; there is no visa on arrival.

faq.question: How much does the Benin eVisa cost?
faq.answer: EUR 50 for a 30-day single-entry visa, EUR 75 for 30-day multiple entry and EUR 100 for a 90-day multiple-entry visa when you apply yourself on evisa.bj (EUR 60, 85 and 110 when applying through an embassy). Approval normally takes a few business days.

faq.question: Is the yellow fever vaccine mandatory for Benin?
faq.answer: No longer at the border. Since September 2026 Benin's Ministry of Health has stopped checking vaccination cards, including yellow fever, at airports, ports and land borders. Vaccination remains recommended for all travelers, and checks can be reinstated in a public health emergency.

faq.question: Can I get a visa on arrival in Benin?
faq.answer: No. Benin replaced its visa-on-arrival scheme with the e-Visa — non-African visitors must hold an approved eVisa before boarding their flight.

faq.question: Is Benin safe to visit?
faq.answer: The south — Cotonou, Ouidah, Porto-Novo, Abomey and the coast — is calmer, though street crime, theft and mugging are common in Cotonou. In the north the FCDO advises against all travel to the W and Pendjari national parks and nearby border areas, and against all but essential travel to the rest of the Alibori and Atacora departments and to the strip between the RNIE 2 highway and the Nigerian border; check current advisories before traveling.
